records.label: Local light only
records.note: Old Baldy's official lighthouse service ended in 1935. Its later unofficial light has no verified modern visibility range, so the map shows a small local marker without a sweeping beam or an assumed 10 nm reach.

records.label: Four grouped sweeps · 10 s cycle
records.note: Oak Island's rotating LED beacon preserves its distinctive group of four flashes followed by a long dark interval. Four grouped beams now illustrate that pattern over a 10-second cycle; their spacing and width are schematic. The current Coast Guard visibility range remains 22 nm.
records.sourceLabel: Friends of Oak Island Lighthouse · rotating LED beacon

records.label: Temporary flashing beacon · every 7.5 s
records.note: During restoration, Hatteras uses a stationary temporary beacon that flashes every 7.5 seconds. The map now pulses instead of rotating; flash duration is illustrative. Its current Coast Guard range is 14 nm. The earlier rotating beacon's 24 nm NPS description predates this equipment change; a replacement Fresnel lens is still planned.

records.label: Steady white light
records.note: Ocracoke has a fixed white light, so its map glow is now steady rather than rotating. It was designed as a secondary coastal light with less powerful optics than Cape Hatteras. The map keeps the current Coast Guard nominal range of 15 nm; glow brightness is illustrative.
records.sourceLabel: National Park Service · Ocracoke Light Station
